Background & Epidemiology.title: Background & Epidemiology
Background & Epidemiology.html:
Not every patient on a radiation service has a cancer you are trying to cure. Much of the day is palliative work (pain, bleeding, obstruction, a spine at risk), emergencies paged in overnight, a smaller group of benign conditions, and radiosurgery for a few non-cancer brain problems. This module covers that work, plus the sites without their own module.

There is no anatomy or staging reading here. Four questions take the place of stage: what is the goal, how long is this patient likely to live, how urgent is it, and what is the least burdensome treatment that reaches the goal?

Four Kinds of Patients

PatientTypical exampleWhat radiation is forWhat usually comes first
PalliativePainful bone metastasis, bleeding bladder tumor, obstructing lung massRelieve or prevent a symptom in as few visits as possibleGoals, prognosis, stability, and the cord
EmergencyCord compression, SVC obstruction, life-threatening bleedingProtect function (walking, breathing) or help stop the eventOften something else: steroids, MRI, a surgeon, a stent, resuscitation, or a biopsy
BenignDupuytren nodules, keloid, heterotopic ossification prevention, painful osteoarthritisSlow overgrowth, prevent recurrence, or relieve painConservative care and consent about long-term risk
Functional or vascular SRSTrigeminal neuralgia, arteriovenous malformation (AVM)A single high dose to a tiny target, with a delayed effectMedication or a multidisciplinary review

Name the Intent Before the Dose

IntentGoalExample
PalliativeRelieve a symptom the patient has now8 Gy in 1 for a painful rib metastasis
ProphylacticPrevent a problem that has not happened yetA high-risk asymptomatic bone metastasis; heterotopic ossification prevention
EmergencyProtect function during an acute threatCord compression, after steroids and surgical review
Ablative or definitiveDurable control of disease, sometimes cureSBRT for a few metastases; 40-50 Gy for a solitary plasmacytoma

Dose ranges overlap across these groups. A benign desmoid tumor may get 50-56 Gy, early-stage follicular lymphoma is treated for cure with 24 Gy, and a palliative bone metastasis may get 30 Gy.

Dose follows the goal and the disease, not the other way around. A low dose can cure a radiosensitive lymphoma, and a high dose can be purely palliative.

What Shapes a Palliative Plan

Palliative Radiation: Who and Why

The most common reason for palliative radiation is a painful bone metastasis. The others are bleeding, obstruction (airway, esophagus, SVC, bowel), and threatened neurologic function from cord compression or brain metastases.

Which Cancers Go to Bone?

Most bone metastases come from prostate, breast, lung, kidney, and thyroid cancer, and multiple myeloma lives in the marrow. They favor the red marrow of the spine, pelvis, ribs, and proximal femur and humerus.

Lesion typeTypical cancersWhy it matters
Blastic (bone-forming, bright on CT)Prostate, some breastShows up well on bone scan
Lytic (bone-destroying, dark on CT)Kidney, thyroid, myeloma, lung, many breastHigher fracture risk; myeloma can be invisible on bone scan
MixedBreast, lungJudge fracture risk by the lytic component
Clinical Pearl

Most patients with bone metastases have them in more than one place. Treat the lesion causing the symptom (and the occasional high-risk lesion), not every spot on the scan.

Benign Disease: Who and Why

Benign radiation is common in Germany and much less common in the United States, and the evidence differs a lot by condition. Broadly, radiation is used to:

Usually below 1 Gy per fraction
Reduce inflammation and pain

Low doses calm inflammatory cells. Used for painful osteoarthritis and plantar fasciitis, where the evidence is debated.

Moderate doses
Stop overgrowth or prevent recurrence

Stop fibroblasts or bone precursor cells from multiplying: early Dupuytren disease, keloids after excision, heterotopic ossification prevention, gynecomastia prevention.

Tumor-level doses
Control a benign tumor

Benign tumors such as desmoid tumors, meningiomas, and vestibular schwannomas get doses similar to cancer treatment.

The Rule for Benign Radiation

1
Alternatives first

Radiation usually comes after, or instead of, other treatments, and only when the benefit justifies it.

2
Smallest effective dose and volume

The lowest dose and smallest field that reach the goal.

3
Long-term risk is part of consent

Any radiation carries a small lifetime risk of a second cancer, highest in younger patients and near the thyroid, breast, eyes, and gonads. Explain it with the alternatives, and document it.

The Rest of the Service

Lymphoma, skin cancer, sarcoma, plasmacytoma and myeloma, pediatric tumors, total body irradiation, and a few smaller sites (bladder, seminoma, thymoma, eye) do not have their own module. The last reading covers each briefly.

High-Yield Summary
  • This service sees four kinds of patients: palliative, emergency, benign, and functional or vascular radiosurgery, and each needs its intent named before its dose.
  • Dose does not define intent: benign tumors can get 50 Gy or more, lymphoma can be cured with 24 Gy, and palliative courses range from one fraction to ten or more.
  • A palliative plan is shaped by the goal, the prognosis, the urgency, the stability of the bone or spine, and the patient's preferences.
  • A painful bone metastasis is the most common reason for palliative radiation, and relief often begins within 1 to 2 weeks, with most responses by 4 to 8 weeks.
  • Benign radiation is offered only when the expected benefit justifies it, at the smallest effective dose and volume, with consent about the small lifetime cancer risk, especially in younger patients.

Workup & Prognosis.title: Workup & Prognosis
Workup & Prognosis.html:
In a curative site, stage tells you the plan. On the palliative service, five questions do that job:

Palliative consult checklist
  • 1. What is the symptom, and is it from this lesion? A hot spot on the scan may not be the cause of the pain.
  • 2. What is the goal? Pain relief, stopping bleeding, walking, preventing a fracture, or durable control. Ask the patient.
  • 3. How long is the patient likely to live? Performance status, primary cancer, sites of disease, and remaining systemic options.
  • 4. Is the bone stable, and is the cord safe? Examine strength, sensation, reflexes, and bladder and bowel function. Mechanical pain, collapse, or any neurologic change needs urgent imaging and a surgical opinion.
  • 5. What has already been treated? Prior radiation to the same area, the dose, and the date. Get the old plan and plan around the cumulative dose; re-irradiation is often still possible.
Stage tells you the plan in curative disease. In palliative disease, the goal, the prognosis, the urgency, and stability tell you the plan.

Goals and Prognosis

Start with what matters to the patient, then estimate prognosis honestly. Clinicians tend to overestimate survival.

Expected survivalWhat it often means for radiation
WeeksA single fraction or no radiation; focus on comfort and hospice
MonthsShort courses (8 Gy in 1, 20 Gy in 5)
Years (or limited disease)30 Gy in 10, or SBRT in selected patients, for durable control

What Predicts Survival

  • Performance status is the most useful single predictor. A patient in bed most of the day (ECOG 3-4) usually has weeks to a few months.
  • Primary cancer: breast and prostate cancer with bone-only disease can live for years; lung cancer with visceral metastases usually much less.
  • Where the metastases are: bone only is better than liver or brain.
  • Systemic options left, such as an effective targeted therapy.
Reference: prognostic scores you might hear named▾
  • Chow three-item model (Chow 2002, validated 2009): non-breast primary, metastases beyond bone, and KPS 60 or less. More factors mean shorter survival.
  • TEACHH (Krishnan 2014).
  • Rades score (cord compression) and the GPA (brain metastases, see CNS).
  • The surprise question ("Would I be surprised if this patient died in the next year?") prompts a goals-of-care conversation.
  • None predicts an individual patient's survival precisely.

Four Kinds of Bone Pain

Tumor and the inflammatory cells around it release prostaglandins and cytokines and drive osteoclasts, which sensitizes nerves in the bone and periosteum. That is biologic pain, and radiation treats it well. As bone is destroyed it weakens until movement causes microfractures or collapse. That is mechanical pain, a structural problem radiation cannot fix. Tumor can also press on a nerve root or the cord.

TypeWhat it feels likeWhat it suggestsUsual next step
BiologicSteady, worse at night, better with steroidsTumor inflammationRadiation and analgesics
MechanicalPain with movement or weight bearing; better lying stillThe bone or spine may be unstableA surgical opinion; RT may follow
Neuropathic (radicular)Shooting pain along a nerve rootNerve root compressionCheck for epidural disease
Neurologic compromiseWeakness, a sensory level, bladder or bowel changeCord or cauda equina compressionEmergency pathway

Imaging: Which Test Answers Which Question

QuestionUsual testWhy
Where are the bone metastases?Bone scan or PET/CT (FDG; PSMA for prostate)Bone scan can miss purely lytic lesions such as myeloma
Will this long bone break?Plain X-rays of the whole bone, then CTHow much of the cortex is destroyed
Is the cord compressed?MRI of the whole spineDisease is often at more than one level
Is the spine stable?CT plus MRICollapse and alignment feed the SINS score

Biopsy if there is no known cancer, if this would be the first metastasis, or if a second cancer, lymphoma, myeloma, or infection is possible. Lymphoma and myeloma are very radiosensitive and often treated with drugs first.

Is the Spine Stable? SINS

SINS, Bilsky, and Mirels organize what you see so you can tell a surgeon. None of them replaces the exam and a multidisciplinary discussion.

The Spinal Instability Neoplastic Score (Fisher 2010) adds six features into a 0-18 score. You do not need the points. Know that a score of 7 or higher should prompt a spine surgery consultation.

  • 0-6: stable.
  • 7-12: potentially unstable. Surgical consultation; many still get radiation alone.
  • 13-18: unstable. Stabilization or cement augmentation is usually considered. Radiation does not restore mechanical stability.

Is the Cord Compressed? Bilsky Grade

The epidural spinal cord compression (ESCC) scale (Bilsky 2010) grades on axial T2 MRI how far tumor has pushed into the canal. Instability and epidural disease are separate problems: a spine can be unstable with an empty canal, or stable with tumor against the cord.

GradeWhat axial T2 MRI showsGroup
0Tumor confined to boneLow grade
1aEpidural tumor without deforming the thecal sacLow grade
1bThecal sac deformed, cord not touchedLow grade
1cTumor abuts the cord without compressing itLow grade (closest to the cord)
2Cord compressed, CSF still visible around itHigh grade
3Cord compressed, no CSF visibleHigh grade

The grade describes the images. Whether the patient has symptoms is a separate question.

Putting It Together: NOMS

Spine teams combine these into the NOMS framework (Laufer 2013): Neurologic, Oncologic, Mechanical, and Systemic.

Will This Long Bone Break? Mirels Score

For a lesion in the femur, humerus, or another long bone, Mirels' score (Mirels 1989) scores site, pain, lesion type, and width involved, each 1-3, for a total of 4-12.

  • 9 or more: high fracture risk. Orthopedics for prophylactic fixation, then postoperative radiation.
  • 8: borderline, a judgment call.
  • 7 or less: lower risk; radiation alone is usually reasonable.

Mirels is sensitive but not very specific: it flags many lesions that would not have broken.

Clinical Pearl

Pain with weight bearing (functional pain) in a lytic femur lesion is a warning sign of impending fracture. Ask about it on every bone consult.

A man with prostate cancer has a painful L3 metastasis. Pain is worst at night, steady, and better on dexamethasone. MRI shows bone disease without epidural extension. Biologic or mechanical pain?

Biologic. Night pain that steroids relieve comes from the tumor and usually responds well to radiation.

A woman with renal cell carcinoma has back pain only when she sits up or stands. CT shows a lytic T12 lesion with 60% collapse. What score do you calculate and who do you call?

SINS: junctional level 3 + mechanical pain 3 + lytic 2 + collapse over 50% 3 = at least 11, before alignment and posterior elements. Call spine surgery: mechanical pain suggests instability, which radiation cannot fix.

A lytic lesion in the mid femoral shaft takes up most of the bone's width and hurts with walking. Mirels score?

Lower limb 2 + functional pain 3 + lytic 3 + more than 2/3 of the width 3 = 11. High fracture risk: orthopedics for prophylactic fixation, then postoperative RT.

A patient with myeloma has new rib pain but a negative bone scan. What do you do?

Bone scan can miss purely lytic myeloma lesions. Get CT, MRI, or PET. Myeloma is very radiosensitive, so low palliative doses usually work well.

High-Yield Summary
  • In palliative care, the goal, the prognosis, the urgency, and the stability of the bone or spine decide the plan, the way stage does in curative disease.
  • Performance status is the most useful predictor of survival, and clinicians tend to overestimate how long patients will live.
  • Mechanical pain suggests instability, which needs a surgical opinion, because radiation does not restore mechanical stability.
  • SINS, the Bilsky grade, and Mirels are decision-support tools: a SINS of 7 or more and a Mirels of 9 or more should prompt a surgical opinion, and Mirels 8 is a judgment call.
  • NOMS combines neurologic compression, tumor radiosensitivity, mechanical stability, and systemic fitness to choose between conventional radiation, SBRT, and surgery.

Palliative Radiation.title: Palliative Radiation
Palliative Radiation.html:
The question is always what is the shortest, simplest course that reaches this patient's goal? For uncomplicated bone pain that is a short course. Durable control, prevention, or limited metastatic disease changes the dose and technique.

Uncomplicated Painful Bone Metastases

Uncomplicated means a painful bone metastasis without impending or completed pathologic fracture, without cord or cauda equina compression, and without prior surgery or radiation to that site. A lesion with any of those is complicated and needs the stability and cord workup first.

For uncomplicated lesions, single and multiple fractions relieve pain about equally well, in RTOG 9714, the Dutch Bone Metastasis Study, and pooled analyses of the randomized trials. What differs is the number of visits, how often retreatment is needed, and short-term side effects.

RegimenVisitsOften chosen whenTrade-off
8 Gy in 11Most uncomplicated lesions, short survival, long travelAbout twice the retreatment
20 Gy in 55Neuropathic pain; many spine lesionsMore visits
30 Gy in 1010Longer survival, after fixation, soft tissue massNo better pain relief

The ASTRO bone metastases guideline (2024) accepts all of these (and 24 Gy in 6) and leaves the choice to shared decision-making on prognosis, performance status, travel, prior radiation, and preference. For pain along a nerve root, many use 20 Gy in 5.

For an uncomplicated painful bone metastasis, 8 Gy in 1, 20 Gy in 5, and 30 Gy in 10 relieve pain about equally. The single fraction trades fewer visits for more retreatment.
RTOG 9714

Breast and prostate cancer bone metastases: 8 Gy in 1 matched 30 Gy in 10 for pain and narcotic relief at 3 months, with less acute toxicity and more retreatment (18% vs 9%).

What to Tell the Patient

  • Timing: keep taking pain medication. No relief at 1 week does not mean it failed.
  • Pain flare in the first days. A few days of dexamethasone lowers it modestly.
  • Side effects depend on the site: nausea (stomach in the field), diarrhea (pelvis), painful swallowing (cervical or upper thoracic spine), fatigue.
  • Retreatment is possible if pain returns (NCIC SC.20), once a new fracture is ruled out.

When the Goal Is More Than Pain Relief

Spine SBRT

SBRT gives a much higher dose in 1-5 treatments with tight margins. Its purpose is durable local control for patients who will live long enough for a conventionally treated lesion to grow back.

Conventional palliative RTSpine SBRT
Typical dose8 Gy in 1, 20 Gy in 5, 30 Gy in 10For example 24 Gy in 2, or a single 16-24 Gy
What it takesSimple planning, often same dayMRI fusion, rigid immobilization, daily imaging, cord carved out
Best fitShort prognosis, many sites, radiosensitive tumorGood performance status, limited disease, radioresistant histology (kidney, melanoma, sarcoma), re-irradiation
Main risksShort-term site effectsVertebral compression fracture, pain flare, rarely myelopathy

ASTRO conditionally recommends SBRT over conventional RT for selected patients: good performance status, no need for surgery, no neurologic symptoms. Two trials show why selection matters:

SC.24

Painful spine metastases (up to 3 consecutive segments, ECOG 0-2, SINS under 12, no symptomatic cord compression): SBRT 24 Gy in 2 gave more complete pain responses at 3 months than 20 Gy in 5 (35% vs 14%).

RTOG 0631

1-3 spine metastases: single-fraction SBRT (16-18 Gy) did not beat 8 Gy in 1 for pain response at 3 months, which was actually higher with 8 Gy (61% vs 41%). Compression fractures and other toxicity were similar.

The trials differed in schedule (two fractions versus one), endpoint (complete response versus a 3-point drop on a 0-10 pain scale), and patients. Higher dose is not automatically better pain relief. SBRT earns its extra work when durable control matters.

  • Epidural disease: SBRT fits low-grade (Bilsky 0-1) disease, with space between tumor and cord. High-grade compression usually means separation surgery first.
  • Instability needs stabilization or cement first.
  • Fracture risk is higher with lytic lesions, existing collapse, and very high single doses.
  • Cord and cauda equina limits shape the plan, which is why immobilization and image guidance matter so much.
Planning details: cord limits▾

Limits vary by protocol. For single-fraction treatment, RTOG 0631 kept the spinal cord under 14 Gy (to 0.03 cc) and the cauda equina under 16 Gy. Prior radiation lowers what the cord can take.

Prophylactic Radiation for High-Risk Bone Metastases

Most asymptomatic bone metastases are watched. A few are likely to fracture, compress the cord, or become painful soon, and treating them early may prevent a skeletal-related event (fracture, cord compression, surgery, or radiation for pain) and a hospitalization.

Gillespie (MSKCC, 2024)

Randomized phase II, 78 patients with more than 5 metastases: radiating asymptomatic high-risk lesions lowered skeletal-related events at 1 year (1.6% vs 29% of lesions) and hospitalizations for them (0 vs 4 patients). Survival was also longer, but that was a secondary endpoint.

"High risk" meant bulky (2 cm or more); at the hip, shoulder, or sacroiliac joint; a third to two-thirds of a long-bone cortex; junctional spine (C7-T1, T12-L1, L5-S1); or posterior vertebral elements. The trial was small and phase III data are pending, so this does not apply to every asymptomatic metastasis. A bulky lesion in a weight-bearing or junctional site deserves a conversation, not automatic observation or treatment.

Oligometastases: When Palliation Becomes Ablation

With only a few metastases, metastasis-directed therapy treats every visible site (usually with SBRT, alongside systemic therapy) for durable control, a break from systemic therapy, or longer survival. It needs a different patient from symptom palliation: good performance status, a controlled primary, and limited disease on modern imaging.

TermMeaning
OligometastaticLimited metastatic disease, usually up to 3-5 lesions
OligorecurrentA few new metastases after the primary was treated
OligoprogressiveA few sites grow while the rest is controlled on systemic therapy
SABR-COMET

Controlled primary and up to 5 metastases: adding SABR improved median overall survival (41 vs 28 months) (randomized phase II with a relaxed significance threshold); 4.5% had a treatment-related death.

The benefit depends on the cancer. SBRT delayed progression and hormone therapy in oligorecurrent prostate cancer, but did not improve survival in oligometastatic breast cancer. Most data are phase II.

Other Palliative Targets

Radiation can relieve bleeding, pain, or obstruction almost anywhere.

SiteCommon indicationsGoalRepresentative regimens
BrainHeadache, seizures, deficitsProtect neurologic functionSRS, or whole-brain 20 Gy in 5 or 30 Gy in 10 (see CNS)
ThoraxHemoptysis, airway obstruction, SVC syndromeStop bleeding, open the airway17 Gy in 2 (a week apart), 20 Gy in 5, 30 Gy in 10; 10 Gy in 1 if frail
Head and neckBleeding, pain, dysphagia, airwayShrink the mass with little toxicityQuad shot: 14.8 Gy in 4 twice-daily fractions over 2 days, repeated about every 4 weeks up to 3 times
GastrointestinalDysphagia, gastric or rectal bleeding, obstruction, liver capsule painStop bleeding, relieve obstruction20 Gy in 5, 30 Gy in 10; whole-liver 8 Gy in 1 for capsule pain
GynecologicVaginal bleeding, pelvic painHemostasis8 Gy in 1 (sometimes repeated), 20 Gy in 5, 30 Gy in 10
GenitourinaryHematuria, pelvic painHemostasis and pain relief20 Gy in 5, 30 Gy in 10
Skin and soft tissueBleeding or fungating massesHemostasis, wound control8 Gy in 1, 20 Gy in 5, 30 Gy in 10

Systemic and Radiopharmaceutical Options

When a cancer carries a target a radioactive drug can find, systemic radiation reaches every lesion at once. Confirm the target on imaging first. These are decided with medical oncology and nuclear medicine.

AgentWhat it targetsWho may receive it
Radium-223Alpha emitter that acts like calcium, taken up where bone turns over around blastic metastasesCastration-resistant prostate cancer with symptomatic bone metastases and no visceral metastases
Lutetium-177 PSMABeta emitter bound to a ligand for prostate-specific membrane antigenCastration-resistant prostate cancer that is PSMA-positive on PET after androgen receptor pathway therapy
Lutetium-177 dotatateBeta emitter bound to a somatostatin analogSomatostatin receptor-positive gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors
Strontium-89, samarium-153Beta emitters taken up in boneDiffuse bone pain; pain relief only, now rarely used

End of Life

Radiation in the last weeks of life is common and often more burden than benefit. Before booking a course, ask:

QuestionWhy it matters
How long is the patient likely to live?Relief takes 1-2 weeks or more
What is the performance status?Bedbound patients have the shortest survival and the hardest trips
What does the patient want?"What are you hoping this treatment will do for you?"
What is the burden?Visits, transport, painful transfers, side effects
Will it change symptoms or quality of life?Not if the symptom has another cause or a faster fix

If radiation still makes sense, give one fraction and involve palliative care and hospice early; a single fraction should not delay hospice. Sometimes the right answer is no radiation.

Reference: other trials you may hear named▾
  • Dutch Bone Metastasis Study: 8 Gy in 1 matched 24 Gy in 6; 25% vs 7% retreated.
  • TROG 96.05 (neuropathic pain): 8 Gy in 1 was not shown to equal 20 Gy in 5 (Roos review).
  • NCIC SC.20 (re-irradiation): 8 Gy in 1 was noninferior to 20 Gy in 5 or 8 by intention to treat, not per protocol.
  • NCIC SC.23: dexamethasone lowered pain flare from 35% to 26%; a later Dutch trial found it delayed flare more than it prevented it.
  • Oligometastases: ORIOLE and STOMP (prostate) and Gomez (NSCLC) were positive; CURB helped NSCLC but not breast cancer; NRG-BR002 (breast) was negative.
  • ALSYMPCA (radium-223), VISION (lutetium-177 PSMA-617), and NETTER-1 (lutetium-177 dotatate) established the radiopharmaceuticals.

A woman with lung cancer, ECOG 4, is admitted with days to weeks to live and a painful hip metastasis. Radiation?

Maybe none. Relief takes 1-2 weeks to start. If she wants to try, one fraction, with hospice involved.

A woman with polymetastatic breast cancer, ECOG 1, has an asymptomatic 3 cm lytic acetabular lesion. Watch or treat?

Discuss prophylactic RT. Bulky and at the hip, it is high risk by the Gillespie definition, but the evidence is phase II.

A man with castration-resistant prostate cancer has painful bone metastases at many sites and new liver metastases. Is radium-223 an option?

No. Radium-223 is for bone metastases without visceral disease. A PSMA PET can show whether lutetium-177 PSMA is an option.

High-Yield Summary
  • For an uncomplicated painful bone metastasis, 8 Gy in 1, 20 Gy in 5, and 30 Gy in 10 relieve pain about equally, but retreatment is about twice as common after a single fraction.
  • Spine SBRT is for durable local control in selected patients, and higher dose is not automatically better pain relief: 24 Gy in 2 beat 20 Gy in 5 in SC.24, but single-fraction SBRT did worse than 8 Gy in 1 in RTOG 0631.
  • The Gillespie phase II trial found that radiating asymptomatic high-risk bone metastases in polymetastatic patients reduced skeletal-related events, but it does not apply to every asymptomatic lesion.
  • Metastasis-directed SBRT for oligometastatic disease helped in SABR-COMET, but the benefit varies by cancer type and setting.
  • Near the end of life, weigh prognosis, performance status, travel, and the time radiation needs to work, and consider one fraction or none.

Oncologic Emergencies.title: Oncologic Emergencies
Oncologic Emergencies.html:
For each emergency, ask what has to happen first, who else needs to be involved, and where radiation fits. Radiation is rarely the first step, and its benefit takes time.

SituationDo firstWhere radiation fitsHow fast radiation helps
Metastatic spinal cord compressionDexamethasone, whole-spine MRI, spine surgery reviewAlone for many; after surgery for othersDays; preserves function more than it restores it
Superior vena cava syndromeAirway, tissue diagnosis, stent if severeAfter diagnosis1-2 weeks or more
Life-threatening bleedingResuscitation, endoscopy, embolizationAlongside or after thoseOften days
Airway obstructionBronchoscopy or stent if criticalDurable reliefDays to weeks
Impending pathologic fractureProtect weight bearing; orthopedicsAfter fixation, or aloneNot an immediate fix
Symptomatic brain metastasesSteroids; surgery for mass effectSRS or whole-brain RTDays to weeks
Before you radiate an emergency, ask what has to happen first: steroids, a scan, a surgeon, a stent, resuscitation, or a biopsy.

Metastatic Spinal Cord Compression

Cord compression is most often from lung, breast, or prostate cancer, then myeloma, lymphoma, and kidney cancer, and most cases are in the thoracic spine. The aim of everything below is to prevent a permanent neurologic deficit.

Recognize It

  • Back pain comes first, often weeks before weakness. New back pain in a patient with cancer deserves a full neurologic exam and a low threshold for MRI.
  • New weakness, a sensory level, or bladder or bowel dysfunction (late) needs same-day evaluation.
  • Ambulatory status before treatment is the strongest predictor of walking afterward. Patients paralyzed for more than a day or two rarely recover.
Patchell (2005)

Selected patients with compression from one area of a non-radiosensitive tumor, not paraplegic for more than 48 hours: direct decompressive surgery then RT kept more patients walking (84% vs 57%) and for longer than RT alone.

Patchell is why a fit patient with single-level, high-grade compression sees a spine surgeon before radiation. It excluded radiosensitive tumors (lymphoma, myeloma, germ cell tumors), which usually go straight to radiation. Without surgery and with a limited prognosis, a single fraction kept patients walking about as well as 20 Gy in 5 (SCORAD III, ICORG 05-03).

Reference: fields and guideline▾
  • The ASTRO bone metastases guideline (2024) favors surgery plus RT over RT alone for selected patients and lists 8 Gy in 1, 16 Gy in 2, 20 Gy in 5, or 30 Gy in 10 without surgery.
  • Fields: the involved vertebrae plus about one level above and below; after surgery, the operated levels and hardware.

Superior Vena Cava Syndrome

Tumor or clot blocks blood returning from the head and arms. Malignant cases are mostly lung cancer (especially small cell) and lymphoma; many others are catheter-related thrombosis.

  • Symptoms: face, neck, and arm swelling, distended chest veins, dyspnea, and headache, worse lying flat.
  • Most patients are not in immediate danger, because collaterals develop over weeks. The true emergencies are stridor or laryngeal edema and confusion from cerebral edema.

Bleeding, Airway, and Fracture

1
Fracture

A completed or impending long-bone fracture needs orthopedic fixation when the patient can tolerate it. Postoperative RT (ASTRO) covers the hardware.

2
Radiation alone

Relieves pain but does not stabilize a broken bone.

A woman with breast cancer has had back pain for 3 weeks and now trips on stairs. Exam shows mild leg weakness and brisk reflexes. First two orders?

Dexamethasone and MRI of the whole spine, now, plus a call to the spine team.

A man with lung cancer has face and arm swelling for 2 weeks. He is breathing comfortably and is alert. CT shows a mediastinal mass. No biopsy yet. Radiate tonight?

No. He is stable, so get tissue first. Small cell or lymphoma gets systemic therapy; a stent is the fast fix if he worsens.

A 55-year-old with renal cell carcinoma has single-level T7 compression (Bilsky 3), has been weak for 12 hours, and can still walk with help. Best approach?

Surgical decompression and stabilization, then RT (Patchell). Renal cell is radioresistant.

A patient with myeloma has cord compression at T10 and can walk. Surgery or radiation?

Usually radiation. Myeloma is highly radiosensitive; surgery is for instability or bone in the canal.

High-Yield Summary
  • Radiation is rarely the first step in an emergency: steroids, imaging, a surgeon, a stent, resuscitation, or a biopsy often come first.
  • For suspected cord compression, give dexamethasone, get an MRI of the whole spine urgently, and involve the spine team, because walking before treatment predicts walking after.
  • Selected fit patients with compression from one area of a tumor that is not very radiosensitive do best with surgery followed by radiation, as shown by Patchell.
  • Patients with cord compression and a limited prognosis can be treated with a single fraction or 20 Gy in 5.
  • In superior vena cava syndrome, protect the airway, stent severely symptomatic patients, and get tissue before radiating, because small cell lung cancer and lymphoma are treated with systemic therapy first.

Benign Disease.title: Benign Disease
Benign Disease.html:
Benign disease radiation covers a wide range of doses and a wide range of evidence. Some indications are supported by randomized trials; others rest on long experience and observational series; a few are genuinely contested. The skill is knowing which condition, at what stage, after which other treatments, and how to talk honestly about the evidence and the small lifetime cancer risk.

Benign radiation is not one thing. Each indication has its own goal, its own dose, and its own quality of evidence, and every consent talk covers the long-term risk.

Long-Term Risk and Consent

1
Age

The lifetime risk of a radiation-induced cancer falls with age, so inflammatory and cosmetic indications are usually reserved for older adults. Be especially cautious in children and younger adults.

2
Location

Keep the thyroid, breast, eyes, and gonads out of the field whenever possible. Hands and feet carry little marrow or organ dose.

3
Alternatives and uncertainty

Explain what else could be done, how strong the evidence is for this condition, and what happens without treatment. Document the conversation.

Heterotopic Ossification

Heterotopic ossification (HO) is bone that forms in soft tissue, most often around the hip after arthroplasty or acetabular fracture surgery, and around the elbow. It can cause pain and stiffness and sometimes needs another operation.

  • Highest risk: prior HO (the strongest predictor), ankylosing spondylitis, diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH), hypertrophic osteoarthritis, and male sex.
  • Why timing is everything: radiation acts on precursor cells before they become bone-forming cells, early around the time of surgery. Once bone has formed, radiation cannot remove it.
  • Regimen: a single 7-8 Gy within about 24 hours before or 72 hours after surgery. In a meta-analysis of randomized trials, radiation was modestly more effective than NSAIDs at preventing severe (Brooker 3-4) HO, the absolute difference was small, and postoperative doses below about 7 Gy worked no better than NSAIDs.
  • Shielding porous implants: some centers block uncemented, porous-coated components from the field to protect bone ingrowth; others do not. A 2022 series found unshielded low-dose preoperative RT did not increase loosening of porous implants. Follow the institutional approach with the orthopedic surgeon.
  • Alternative: NSAIDs such as indomethacin, which carry GI bleeding and kidney risks and need several days to weeks of dosing.

Keloids

  • Keloids are scars that grow beyond the original wound. Excision alone often fails, sometimes with a larger keloid.
  • Postoperative RT, usually started within about a day or two of excision, lowers recurrence. In a meta-analysis of 72 studies, recurrence averaged about 22% with surgery plus RT, versus 37% with RT alone; chest keloids recurred most.
  • Electrons, superficial X-rays, or brachytherapy to the scar with a small margin. Regimens vary widely (for example 12-16 Gy in 3-4 fractions), with higher doses sometimes used at high-tension sites such as the chest and shoulder.
  • Side effects are mostly pigment changes. Avoid in children when possible, and discuss the small long-term cancer risk, especially near the breast or thyroid.

Gynecomastia Prevention

Men with prostate cancer who take an antiandrogen alone (for example high-dose bicalutamide, now uncommon) often develop painful breast enlargement. A single low dose to each breast bud before starting the drug reduces it: in a sham-controlled trial, 10 Gy cut gynecomastia from 85% to 52%. In a head-to-head trial, tamoxifen prevented it more effectively than 12 Gy of radiation (8% vs 34%, compared with 69% with no prevention), so radiation is mainly for men who cannot take tamoxifen. Treatment after the breast has grown works poorly.

Dupuytren and Ledderhose Disease

Dupuytren disease is a fibroproliferative disorder of the palmar fascia: first nodules, then cords, then flexion contracture of the fingers (ring and little fingers most often). Ledderhose disease is the same process in the sole of the foot.

Early: nodules and cords, little or no contracture
Radiation may slow progression

Radiation targets proliferating fibroblasts. In a randomized comparison of two schedules, about 90% of treated hands were stable or improved at 1 year, but there was no untreated control group.

Late: established contracture
Procedures

Needle aponeurotomy, collagenase (where available), or surgery straighten the finger. Radiation cannot reverse a mature contracture.

  • How good is the evidence? Modest. NICE IPG573 (2016) judged the efficacy evidence inadequate, partly because early Dupuytren disease does not always progress on its own, and recommends radiation only with special arrangements for consent and audit.
  • Technique: low-energy X-rays (orthovoltage) or electrons to the nodules and cords with a margin of about 1-2 cm, the rest of the hand shielded.
  • Regimen: about 30 Gy in two courses of 5 x 3 Gy separated by 6-12 weeks, or 21 Gy in 7 fractions.
  • Side effects: dry skin and mild redness acutely; late dryness, thinning, or altered sensation in a small minority.
Clinical Pearl

The key word for Dupuytren radiation is early: a patient who can still lay the hand flat on a table (a negative tabletop test). Even then, describe the benefit as possible slowing of progression, not a guarantee.

Osteoarthritis and Plantar Fasciitis

  • Who: older adults with chronic joint or heel pain that has not responded to exercise, analgesics, injections, physical therapy, orthotics, or weight loss, or who are poor surgical candidates.
  • How: very low doses, often 0.5-1 Gy two to three times a week, 3-6 Gy total, sometimes repeated after 6-12 weeks.
  • Side effects: essentially none acutely at these doses.
Mahler (osteoarthritis sham trials)

Two Dutch randomized trials, knee and hand osteoarthritis: 6 x 1 Gy was no better than sham radiation for pain or function, at 3 months or at 12 months. The placebo effect in joint pain is large.

Niewald

Plantar fasciitis: 6 x 1 Gy relieved heel pain better than a very low 6 x 0.1 Gy control. There was no sham arm, and a later trial found 0.5 Gy and 1 Gy per fraction equivalent.

If asked, say that low-dose RT for osteoarthritis is contested: German and other European centers use it widely, but the only sham-controlled trials were negative, and they were small. For plantar fasciitis the randomized data compare doses rather than radiation with no radiation. Either way, it is an option only after conservative care fails, with an honest discussion of uncertain benefit and small long-term risk.

Other Benign Conditions You May Hear About

ConditionWhere radiation fits
Graves orbitopathyThe EUGOGO guideline (2021) lists orbital RT, combined with steroids, as a second-line option for active moderate-to-severe disease. Avoid in diabetic retinopathy and be cautious in younger patients; newer drugs such as teprotumumab have changed practice.
PterygiumA single beta-ray dose after excision lowered recurrence in a randomized trial. Higher doses can thin the sclera; many surgeons use autografts or mitomycin C instead.
Desmoid tumorActive surveillance or systemic therapy first; RT (about 50-56 Gy) for progressive or symptomatic disease when surgery would be morbid. Response is slow, sometimes over years (EORTC 62991).
Epicondylitis, shoulder syndromesLow-dose anti-inflammatory RT, similar to osteoarthritis, with similar uncertainty
Benign tumors (meningioma, vestibular schwannoma, pituitary adenoma, paraganglioma)Fractionated RT or SRS at tumor-control doses; see the CNS module

A 70-year-old has painful nodules in both palms and can still lay her hands flat. Radiation?

It is an option. Early Dupuytren disease: about 30 Gy in two split courses may slow progression. Explain that the evidence is limited and early disease does not always progress.

A 64-year-old has a ring finger fixed at 60 degrees of flexion from a thick cord. Radiation?

No. RT cannot reverse an established contracture. Refer for needle aponeurotomy, collagenase, or surgery.

A man who developed HO after his left hip replacement is scheduled for a right hip replacement next week. What do you offer, and when?

A single 7-8 Gy within about 24 hours before or 72 hours after surgery, or NSAID prophylaxis. Prior HO is the strongest risk factor.

A 35-year-old asks for radiation for knee osteoarthritis. What do you weigh?

Her age and the evidence. The lifetime cancer risk is higher in younger patients, and sham-controlled trials were negative. Other treatment is preferred.

High-Yield Summary
  • Benign radiation covers very different doses and very different levels of evidence, so each indication needs its own justification.
  • Heterotopic ossification is prevented with a single 7 to 8 Gy within about a day before or 3 days after surgery, with randomized evidence behind it.
  • Dupuytren disease is treated only in its early stage, and the evidence that radiation slows progression is limited.
  • Low-dose radiation for osteoarthritis is contested, because sham-controlled trials did not show a benefit.
  • Every benign consent covers the alternatives, the uncertainty, and the small lifetime cancer risk, which is highest in younger patients and near the thyroid, breast, eyes, and gonads.

Functional & Vascular Radiosurgery.title: Functional & Vascular Radiosurgery
Functional & Vascular Radiosurgery.html:
Radiosurgery is not only for tumors. Two non-cancer brain conditions come up again and again: trigeminal neuralgia and arteriovenous malformations (AVMs). Both use a single, very precise, very high dose, and in both the benefit is delayed, on very different time scales.

Trigeminal neuralgia
Target: a nerve

A tiny spot on the trigeminal nerve root gets about 70-90 Gy maximum dose. Pain relief usually takes weeks.

AVM
Target: a tangle of vessels

The whole nidus gets about 16-25 Gy at its edge. The vessels close over 1-3 years or more.

In functional and vascular radiosurgery, the effect is delayed. Pain relief takes weeks; AVM closure takes years, and the patient is not fully protected until it happens.

Trigeminal Neuralgia

Recognize It

  • Brief, electric shock-like, one-sided facial pain lasting seconds, usually in the V2 or V3 distribution (cheek, jaw).
  • Triggered by light touch, chewing, talking, brushing teeth, or wind. Between attacks the patient is usually pain free and the neurologic exam is normal.
  • Most patients are over 50 and more are women. In a young patient, with bilateral symptoms, or with sensory loss, think of a secondary cause such as multiple sclerosis or a tumor.
  • The usual cause is a blood vessel (most often the superior cerebellar artery) pressing on the nerve near where it enters the pons.

Workup and First-Line Treatment

  • MRI with thin-slice sequences to exclude a tumor or MS and to look for a compressing vessel.
  • Carbamazepine (or oxcarbazepine) is first-line and works for most patients at first. Procedures are for pain that drugs no longer control or side effects the patient cannot tolerate.
ProcedureOften best forTrade-off
Microvascular decompressionHealthier patients with a compressing vesselMost durable relief, but a craniotomy
Percutaneous rhizotomy (glycerol, balloon, radiofrequency)Patients who need immediate reliefQuick, but numbness and recurrence are common
Stereotactic radiosurgeryOlder or medically frail patients, those on anticoagulants, or after other procedures failNoninvasive, but relief is delayed and recurrence is common over years

Radiosurgery Details

  • Target: the trigeminal nerve root in the cistern with a single small (4 mm) shot. Centers differ on how close to the pons they aim; a target farther from the brainstem tends to give more relief and more numbness.
  • Dose: a maximum dose of about 70-90 Gy (median 80 Gy in a large series) in one session, prescribed to the center of the tiny target, not to an edge.
  • Response: in the large multicenter series, about 80% had initial relief at a median of about a month; about 4 in 10 of them later had pain return (median about 3.5 years). Repeat SRS is possible.
  • Main side effect: new facial numbness in roughly a quarter of patients, appearing months later. Severe painful numbness (anesthesia dolorosa) is rare.
Reference: Barrow Neurological Institute (BNI) pain score▾

Outcomes are reported on the BNI scale: I no pain, no medication; II occasional pain, no medication; IIIa no pain on medication; IIIb some pain, adequately controlled on medication; IV some pain, not adequately controlled; V severe pain, no relief. "Success" is usually BNI I-IIIa or I-IIIb, depending on the study.

Arteriovenous Malformations

An AVM is a tangle of abnormal vessels (the nidus) where arteries connect directly to veins without capillaries in between. The high-pressure flow can rupture.

Recognize It

  • Hemorrhage is the most common presentation, usually in a young adult; then seizures, headache, or a focal deficit. Many are found by chance on MRI.
  • The risk of bleeding is roughly 2-4% per year on average, higher after a prior bleed and with deep location, deep venous drainage, or an associated aneurysm.
  • Catheter angiography is the gold standard to map the feeding arteries, nidus, and draining veins.

Spetzler-Martin Grade

FeaturePoints
Size: under 3 cm / 3-6 cm / over 6 cm1 / 2 / 3
Eloquent brain nearby (motor, sensory, language, visual cortex, thalamus, hypothalamus, brainstem): no / yes0 / 1
Venous drainage: superficial only / any deep0 / 1

The Spetzler-Martin grade (I-V) estimates surgical risk. In general, low grades (I-II) often go to surgery, which closes the AVM immediately; small AVMs in deep or eloquent locations are the classic radiosurgery patients; grade III needs individual judgment; and high grades (IV-V) are often observed. The grade is a starting point, not a decision: rupture history, age, anatomy (aneurysms, venous drainage), and the risk of each option are weighed by a multidisciplinary team of neurosurgery, neurointerventional radiology, and radiation oncology.

Radiosurgery Details

  • Who: usually small AVMs (often under about 3 cm, or about 10 cc) in deep or eloquent brain.
  • Dose: about 16-25 Gy to the edge of the nidus in one session. Higher doses close more AVMs but cause more injury to the surrounding brain.
  • How it works: radiation injures the vessel lining, which slowly thickens until the vessels close. Complete obliteration usually takes 1-3 years and occurs in roughly 70-80% of small AVMs.
  • The latency period: in a large series, bleeding risk fell by about half after radiosurgery even before obliteration, and fell much further after obliteration, but was not zero in either period. Patients need to understand this.
  • Follow-up: MRI every 6-12 months, then angiography to confirm obliteration, usually around 3 years.
  • Side effects: imaging changes around the treated area are common; symptomatic swelling, seizures, or late cysts occur in a minority.
ARUBA

Unruptured brain AVMs: the trial was stopped early when medical management alone had fewer deaths or strokes than medical management plus intervention (10% vs 31%, mean follow-up about 33 months).

ARUBA is widely debated: follow-up was short compared with a young patient's lifetime risk, interventions were mixed (embolization, surgery, radiosurgery), relatively few patients had surgery, and selection may not reflect experienced centers. It made observation a real option for unruptured AVMs; it did not settle the question for every patient.

Clinical Pearl

Ruptured AVMs are usually treated, because the risk of bleeding again is highest early. For unruptured AVMs, the decision weighs a long lifetime of small annual risk (higher in young patients) against the immediate risk of treatment.

Other Functional Radiosurgery

  • Essential tremor and tremor-dominant Parkinson disease: Gamma Knife thalamotomy (a very high single dose to the ventral intermediate nucleus) for patients who cannot have deep brain stimulation or focused ultrasound. The effect is delayed by months.
  • Cardiac radioablation for refractory ventricular tachycardia (a single 25 Gy to the arrhythmia substrate) is an emerging, investigational use.

A 72-year-old on warfarin has electric shock-like right jaw pain when she chews. Carbamazepine now makes her too drowsy. MRI shows no tumor. Which procedure fits her best?

Stereotactic radiosurgery is a good fit: noninvasive, no need to stop anticoagulation, and suited to an older patient. Relief takes weeks.

What is the main side effect to counsel her about?

New facial numbness, in roughly a quarter of patients, often months later.

A 28-year-old has a 2.2 cm AVM in the left thalamus with deep venous drainage that bled 2 months ago. Spetzler-Martin grade, and a reasonable option?

Size 1 + eloquent 1 + deep drainage 1 = grade III. Deep, eloquent location makes surgery risky, so SRS is a reasonable option after multidisciplinary review.

Six months after SRS, the AVM above is smaller but still fills on MRA. Is he protected from bleeding?

Not fully. Risk is lower during the latency period but not gone, and it falls further only after complete obliteration, which usually takes 1-3 years.

High-Yield Summary
  • Trigeminal neuralgia causes brief, electric shock-like facial pain in the V2 or V3 distribution, and carbamazepine is the first-line treatment.
  • Radiosurgery for trigeminal neuralgia gives a maximum dose of about 70 to 90 Gy to the nerve root, relief usually starts within about a month, and new facial numbness is the main side effect.
  • The Spetzler-Martin grade estimates surgical risk from AVM size, eloquent location, and deep venous drainage, but treatment is chosen by a multidisciplinary team.
  • After AVM radiosurgery, the vessels close over 1 to 3 years, and bleeding risk is lower but not gone until obliteration is confirmed.
  • ARUBA favored medical management for unruptured AVMs over its short follow-up, which made observation a real option without settling every case.

Other Sites in Brief.title: Other Sites in Brief
Other Sites in Brief.html:
These sites do not have their own module, but they appear on the schedule and on exams. For each one: where does radiation fit, and what is the one rule or trial to know? Treat these as orientation. Stage, patient selection, institutional practice, and new evidence change the details, and each site has its own guideline.

Lymphoma

Lymphomas are very radiosensitive, so doses are low (often 20-36 Gy) and radiation is usually given after chemotherapy as consolidation, or alone for some early indolent lymphomas. Fields have shrunk from large extended fields to involved-site RT (ISRT), which treats only the originally involved sites, to cut late effects.

DiseaseWhere radiation fitsKnow
Early Hodgkin lymphomaShort chemotherapy (ABVD) then ISRT: 20 Gy for favorable disease, 30 Gy for unfavorableGHSG HD10/HD11 set those doses. PET-adapted trials (RAPID, H10, HD16): omitting RT after a negative interim PET slightly increased relapse without a clear survival difference, so the decision is individualized.
Diffuse large B-cell lymphomaR-CHOP, then RT to bulky disease or residual PET-positive disease in many patients (often 30-36 Gy)Younger patients with early, non-bulky, low-risk disease can often be treated with chemotherapy alone (FLYER)
Follicular lymphoma, early stageISRT 24 Gy alone can give long-term controlFORT: 24 Gy controlled disease better than 4 Gy
Indolent lymphoma, palliative4 Gy in 2 ("boom-boom") relieves symptomsVery low dose, high response
Gastric MALT lymphomaH. pylori eradication first; RT (about 24-30 Gy) if lymphoma persists or is H. pylori negativeHighly curable with RT
Mycosis fungoidesLocal RT for plaques; total skin electron beam for widespread skin diseaseEven single low doses work for individual lesions
Clinical Pearl

Why fields shrank: survivors of Hodgkin lymphoma treated with large mantle fields as young women had high rates of breast cancer, heart disease, and hypothyroidism decades later.

Skin Cancer

  • Basal and squamous cell carcinoma: surgery (often Mohs) is standard. Definitive RT is an alternative, especially for older patients and for the nose, eyelid, lip, and ear, where surgery would cost function or cosmesis.
  • Adjuvant RT after surgery for squamous cell carcinoma is considered for perineural invasion of a named or large nerve, positive margins that cannot be re-excised, or nodal disease.
  • Be cautious in young patients (late cosmetic changes), on the lower leg (poor healing), in genetic syndromes that sensitize to radiation (Gorlin, xeroderma pigmentosum), and in some connective tissue diseases.
  • Merkel cell carcinoma: aggressive and very radiosensitive; excision with sentinel node biopsy, then RT to the tumor bed (and often the nodes) for many patients.
  • Melanoma: adjuvant nodal RT lowered lymph-node field relapse without improving survival (ANZMTG/TROG); it is used much less in the immunotherapy era. RT is common for melanoma brain metastases (see CNS).

Regimens range from about 50-66 Gy in 20-33 fractions to shorter courses (for example 35 Gy in 5 or 40 Gy in 10) for frail patients.

Soft Tissue Sarcoma

For extremity sarcoma, limb-sparing surgery plus radiation replaced amputation in most patients. The question is whether to give radiation before or after surgery.

Preoperative
About 50 Gy in 25

Smaller field and lower dose, so less permanent fibrosis, edema, and joint stiffness, but more wound complications. Now commonly preferred.

Postoperative
About 60-66 Gy

Fewer wound problems, but a larger, higher-dose field and more permanent late effects.

NCIC SR2 (O'Sullivan)

Extremity sarcoma: preoperative and postoperative RT gave similar local control; preoperative RT had about twice the major wound complications (35% vs 17%), and postoperative RT more late fibrosis.

STRASS

Retroperitoneal sarcoma: preoperative RT did not improve abdominal recurrence-free survival overall.

Plasmacytoma and Myeloma

  • Solitary plasmacytoma (one lesion, no myeloma): definitive RT, about 35-50 Gy depending on site and size, controls the lesion in most patients, though many solitary bone plasmacytomas later progress to myeloma.
  • Multiple myeloma: radiation is palliative and low doses work (for example 8 Gy in 1 or 20 Gy in 5). Keep fields small to protect marrow for future therapy and stem cell collection.

Pediatrics

Children are the most sensitive patients to late effects: growth, cognition, hormones, fertility, and second cancers. That is why pediatric plans use the lowest effective dose, often use protons, and young children often need daily anesthesia to lie still. Treatment follows cooperative-group protocols.

TumorWhere radiation fits
MedulloblastomaCraniospinal RT plus a posterior fossa or tumor-bed boost after surgery (see CNS)
Wilms tumorLow-dose flank RT for higher-stage disease; whole-lung RT for lung metastases that do not fully respond to chemotherapy
RhabdomyosarcomaRT for most patients except those with completely resected, favorable tumors
Ewing sarcomaRadiosensitive; RT when surgery would be too morbid or margins are positive
Hodgkin lymphomaResponse-adapted: RT omitted for many children who respond well to chemotherapy

Total Body Irradiation

TBI is part of the conditioning regimen before some allogeneic stem cell transplants (most often for leukemia): it kills leukemia cells, including those in sanctuary sites, and suppresses the immune system so the donor graft can take. Myeloablative regimens commonly give about 12-13.2 Gy in 6-8 twice-daily fractions; non-myeloablative regimens give as little as 2 Gy. The lungs are the main dose-limiting organ (pneumonitis), so they are often partly shielded.

Also on the Schedule

SiteWhere radiation fitsKnow
BladderTrimodality therapy (maximal TURBT, then chemoradiation) as a bladder-sparing alternative to cystectomy in selected patientsBC2001: adding chemotherapy to RT improved locoregional control
Testicular seminoma, stage ISurveillance is preferred for most; para-aortic RT (20 Gy) or single-dose carboplatin are alternativesVery radiosensitive; MRC TE18 showed 20 Gy matched 30 Gy
ThymomaPostoperative RT considered for incompletely resected or more invasive tumors; its role in completely resected early tumors is debatedMyasthenia gravis is a common association
Uveal melanomaPlaque brachytherapy for medium tumors preserves the eyeCOMS: similar survival to enucleation
Renal cell carcinomaSBRT for primary tumors in selected patients who cannot have surgery (mostly phase II data), and for metastasesRadioresistant to conventional doses, but responds to ablative doses
High-Yield Summary
  • Lymphoma is very radiosensitive, so involved-site radiation uses low doses, usually after chemotherapy, and early follicular lymphoma can be controlled with 24 Gy alone.
  • Radiation is a good alternative to surgery for basal and squamous cell skin cancers of the nose, eyelid, lip, and ear, especially in older patients.
  • Preoperative radiation for extremity sarcoma causes more wound complications, while postoperative radiation causes more permanent fibrosis and stiffness.
  • A solitary plasmacytoma is treated definitively with about 35 to 50 Gy, while myeloma needs only low palliative doses.
  • Children are the most vulnerable to late effects, so pediatric radiation uses the lowest effective dose, often protons, and cooperative-group protocols.
